questions.question: According to the course, what is the main difference between a résumé and a portfolio?
choices: A résumé is longer and more detailed than a portfolio
The difference is proof—a portfolio shows evidence of impact, while a résumé only lists experience
A portfolio is always digital, while a résumé can be printed
A résumé is for job applications, while a portfolio is only for freelancers
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—a portfolio answers the question with proof by showing the problem, your solution, the results, and what you learned.
questions.feedback_incorrect: While format and audience differ, the core distinction is that a portfolio demonstrates proof of impact with context, while a résumé simply lists what you've done. A hiring manager reading a portfolio should move from doubt to confidence.

questions.question: What are the three things a strong positioning statement should answer?
choices: Your education, previous employers, and salary expectations
Who you help, what specific problem you solve, and why that matters
Your years of experience, certifications, and technical skills
Your career goals, preferred work environment, and personal interests
questions.feedback_correct: That's right—a positioning statement is your elevator pitch that immediately clarifies who you serve and the value you bring.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A positioning statement is concise and audience-focused, not a full history or personal preferences. It should quickly explain who you help, what you solve for them, and why your work matters.

questions.question: What are the six benchmarks that define a strong first portfolio site according to Slide 13?
choices: Colorful design, fast loading, mobile-responsive, SEO-optimized, social media integration, and analytics tracking
Easy to Scan, Specific, Honest, Audience-Aware, Evidence-Based, and Clear Next Steps
Professional headshot, extensive work history, multiple testimonials, high word count, and interactive features
Unique domain name, multiple portfolio pages, video content, client logos, and awards section
questions.feedback_correct: Perfect—these six benchmarks emphasize clarity and functionality over flashiness, and they're what actually influence visitor decisions.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A strong portfolio prioritizes substance and clarity over design features. The benchmarks focus on making your work scannable, specific, truthful, and aligned with what your audience actually needs to see.

questions.question: Before making changes to your first portfolio version, what does Slide 7 suggest you should do?
choices: Immediately update all generic-sounding sections with more personal language
Ask friends and family for feedback before making any edits
Step back and ask five critical evaluation questions to identify what's strong and what needs work
Rebuild the entire site from scratch with a different approach
questions.feedback_correct: Spot-on—resist the urge to immediately edit and instead evaluate objectively using those five questions: What feels strong? Generic? Missing? Too long? And what would a visitor understand in 30 seconds?
questions.feedback_incorrect: The key principle is diagnosis before editing. Taking time to step back and objectively evaluate your site prevents wasting effort on low-impact changes and helps you focus on what actually matters most to visitors.

questions.question: According to Slide 5, what three categories of materials should you gather before building your portfolio?
choices: Social media accounts, email contacts, and work references
Professional headshots, video clips, and podcast recordings
Career Documents, Work Evidence, and Personal Assets
Job descriptions, salary history, and performance reviews
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—these three categories include everything from your résumé to your testimonials to your professional photo, and you likely already have most of it.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The course emphasizes that you don't need to create new materials from scratch. The three categories—Career Documents (résumé, bio), Work Evidence (projects, samples, credentials), and Personal Assets (headshot, contact info)—cover what you already have on hand.

questions.question: What does Slide 9 identify as the core question every portfolio must answer within the first 30 seconds?
choices: What is your educational background and where did you study?
How much experience do you have in your field?
Why should this person be trusted with important work?
What are your salary requirements and benefits expectations?
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—establishing trust immediately is the core purpose of your portfolio, and you have about 30 seconds before a visitor makes a judgment.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Your portfolio's job is to build confidence in your trustworthiness and capability. While experience and background matter, they're supporting details, not the main message you need to lead with.

questions.question: According to Slide 11, what is the critical constraint when applying improvements to your portfolio to maintain authenticity?
choices: Make as many changes as possible in one editing session to save time
Add more client testimonials and impressive metrics to stand out
Focus on the three highest-impact improvements while maintaining your authentic voice and avoiding invented or exaggerated claims
Redesign the entire layout to look more modern and trendy
questions.feedback_correct: That's right—the balanced approach ensures meaningful improvements without overdoing it or sacrificing credibility through embellishment.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The course emphasizes that authenticity is non-negotiable. Making high-impact changes is good, but not if it means inventing metrics, creating fake clients, or exaggerating your role. Quality and honesty beat quantity and embellishment every time.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of the three-pass editing approach described in Slide 12?
choices: To find spelling and grammar errors before publishing
To create three completely different versions of your portfolio
To refine your portfolio through three focused passes—each with a single goal of clarifying message, improving layout, and strengthening proof
To get three rounds of feedback from external reviewers
questions.feedback_correct: Correct—this deliberate, methodical approach prevents trying to fix everything at once and ensures each pass targets a specific improvement area.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The three-pass method is about focused, sequential refinement, not about creating alternatives or external feedback loops. Each pass has a clear, singular goal that builds on the previous work.

questions.question: According to Slide 22, what does a Portfolio AI Teammate help you do on an ongoing basis?
choices: Replace you at networking events and client meetings
Capture new accomplishments as they happen, help create case studies, customize versions for different audiences, and keep your portfolio current over time
Generate fake accomplishments and exaggerated metrics to impress visitors
Handle all your email communications and schedule your calendar
questions.feedback_correct: Perfect—the AI Teammate is a long-term asset that evolves with your career and ensures your portfolio stays fresh and relevant, not a one-time course tool.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The AI Teammate serves as a continuous career partner that helps you maintain and personalize your portfolio over time. It's about capturing accomplishments when they're fresh and adapting your story for different audiences—not a replacement for you.
